passage: The kabaddi final at the Shivpur school ground ended at dusk, and Uday's team had won. He scanned the crowd one more time. No Harsha. Harsha had promised, twice, and had even said he'd bring the dhol. On the walk home past the sugarcane fields, Uday's cousin asked where his friend was. 'Friend? He's a fake,' Uday said. 'A total loser. Always was.' He kicked a clod of mud. His cousin said, 'Harsha? The one who sat up with you before your board exam?' 'That was then. He's fake.' Uday didn't want to think about the exam night, or the dhol, or anything. The word 'fake' was easier. It shut the whole subject like a door. When Harsha's name flashed on his phone that evening, he turned it face down without answering.

qa.q: What had Harsha said he would bring to the final?
qa.a: Harsha had said he'd bring the dhol.

qa.q: Why is 'fake' easier for Uday than thinking about the exam night?
qa.a: Uday is hurt and let down on a day that should have been happy, and one harsh word lets him skip the confusing mix of hurt and past kindness; it shuts the subject like a door.

qa.q: What could Uday do instead of turning the phone face down?
qa.a: Uday could answer, say he was hurt that Harsha missed the final, and ask what happened, which leaves room for an explanation and repair.

qa.q: What might Harsha be feeling when the call isn't answered?
qa.a: Harsha may already feel guilty about missing the final and now worried or confused, not knowing Uday has decided he is 'fake'.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, let down by a friend at his kabaddi final, calls him a fake and a loser and refuses to think about anything else.

passage: In the corridor of their school in Malmö, Emil read the science-fair list pinned by the lab: Priscila was in Group 4, with Johan and Vera. Not with him. They had talked about their water-filter idea for weeks. At lunch he told Axel, 'She's such a fake. A total loser, honestly. Uses people and drops them.' Axel raised an eyebrow. 'Priscila? She lent you her notes for a whole month when you had flu.' Emil stabbed a meatball. 'Whatever. That's what fakes do.' He could feel the other things trying to get in, the notes, the bus rides, the time she laughed at his terrible joke, and he shut them out. It was simpler to have one word for her. That afternoon, when Priscila waved at him across the hall, he looked straight through her.

qa.q: Which group was Priscila in on the science-fair list?
qa.a: Priscila was in Group 4, with Johan and Vera.

qa.q: Why does Emil push away memories like the notes and the bus rides?
qa.a: Emil feels let down, and those memories don't fit 'fake', so letting them in would mean feeling confused and hurt instead of simply angry.

qa.q: What small step could Emil try before deciding Priscila is fake?
qa.a: He could ask Priscila how the groups were made and say he was disappointed, which invites the rest of the story instead of ending it.

qa.q: How might Priscila feel when Emil looks straight through her?
qa.a: Priscila may feel confused and hurt, especially if there was a reason for the group change that Emil never asked about.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, disappointed about a science-fair group, labels a friend a fake and a loser and shuts out everything else he knows about her.

passage:
Bhupen,

I'm writing this because I can't say it to your face without shouting.

You promised you'd come to my kathak recital. You PROMISED. I looked for you in the third row the whole time. Then Nisha tells me you were at the mall with Ronak's group.

So now I know what you are. You're a fake. A total loser. All those times you walked me home from tuition, you were probably just bored. The birthday card you made me with the peacock, probably Ronak's idea too. You're just a fake person, and I don't need to know why you did it, because I already know.

Don't bother explaining.

Sabina

(I haven't sent this yet. Ammi says to sleep on it. But I don't see what sleeping will change. A fake is a fake.)

qa.a: At the mall with Ronak's group.

qa.a: Sabina is hurt and let down, and the label gives the anger a simple shape. It also means Sabina doesn't have to wonder why Bhupen really didn't come.

qa.a: Sabina could ask Bhupen what happened and say plainly how much it hurt that Bhupen missed the recital. That leaves room for an explanation or an apology, which the label shuts out.

qa.a: Bhupen would probably feel attacked and confused, especially at having the walks home and the peacock card thrown back. Bhupen might get defensive instead of apologising.

Didi, you're asking about Eshaan? Don't. I'm Chinmay, and I'm done with him.

You know what he did? We had a plan: Saturday, science model, his house. I carried my whole volcano on the bus. Paint, soda, everything. And when I got there, his mother said he'd gone to the cricket nets with the Class 10 boys.

So that's who he is. A fake. A loser who drops people for seniors. I don't care about anything else he's done.

What? Don't give me that look, I'm your brother, I know that look. Yes, he helped me with maths all of last term. So? And he sat with me when my grandfather died. That was then. Now I know the real Eshaan.

He's been messaging. Six times. I haven't opened any of them. Why would I? I know what they say. Excuses.

...Okay, I'll look at one. Just to see how fake the excuse is.

qa.a: He'd gone to the cricket nets with the Class 10 boys.

qa.a: He is hurt and has already decided Eshaan is a fake, so he believes he knows what the messages say. The label saves him from having to think about Eshaan's side.

qa.a: Deciding to look at one message. Even if it's out of suspicion, reading it gives Eshaan a chance to explain and brings back some curiosity.

qa.a: Didi probably understands the hurt but also remembers Eshaan helping with maths and sitting with Chinmay after the grandfather's death. Didi may want to nudge Chinmay to hear the other side.
